title: How Murphy's Law Works, the Redux
summary: Josh and Chuck revisit Murphy's Law, an expanded remake of an earlier short episode. They cover the idiom's roots: Sod's Law in Great Britain, Adam Holoshirk's 1949-era magic essay line about things going wrong, and Captain Edward A. Murphy Jr., an Air Force engineer. The main story is the 1949 Edwards Air Force Base rocket sled tests (Project MX-981) on human tolerance to G-force, where John Paul Stapp rode the sled, and where a miswired sensor set-up led Murphy to grumble the principle, which Stapp then popularized at a press conference. They discuss the 1950s-60s wave of pithy "unnatural laws" (Peter Principle, Parkinson's Law, Boob's law, Lincoln's law, Patton's law), how Murphy's Law spurred fail-safe and redundant engineering, seatbelt advocacy, fatalism versus free will, the buttered bread "Murphy" example, Joel Pell's 2005 "Murphy's equation," and closing listener Facebook/Twitter Q&A with personal anecdotes.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener Q&A

segments.title: Reboot of the Murphy's Law episode
segments.summary: Josh explains he pitched and redid the Murphy's Law episode, which was too short the first time, and frames the idiom and the human tendency to focus on negatives.

segments.title: Origins: Sod's Law and Adam Holloway
segments.summary: Discussion of Sod's Law in Great Britain and a magician's essay line (attributed to Adam Holloway, spelled Hole Shirk in the transcript) that nine out of ten things that can go wrong usually will. Murphy's Law was not coined by Murphy; Murphy is a captain in the Air Force who died in 1990.

segments.title: Rocket sled tests at Edwards
segments.summary: Set the scene at Edwards Air Force Base in 1949. Project MX-981 tested how the human body handled G-force, since planes were designed around a supposed eighteen-G limit. Cadavers, then dummies like Sierra Sam and Oscar Eight Ball were used before John Paul Stapp volunteered.

segments.title: John Paul Stapp and the 46.2 G ride
segments.summary: Stapp rode the sled reaching about 200 mph and stopping in under a second, withstanding 18 Gs, then 20, and up to 46.2 Gs. He suffered broken bones, concussions, broken blood vessels in the eyes, and blackouts and redouts. He also pushed for seatbelts and staged early car crash tests.

segments.title: Miswired sensors and the birth of the saying
segments.summary: Murphy arrived with more accurate sensors; an assistant hooked them up incorrectly, and Murphy grumbled that if something can go wrong it will. Witnesses describe him as rude, though his son disputes that. Stapp used the line at a press conference, where it got a laugh and spread through aerospace publications.

segments.title: 1950s unnatural laws and fail-safe engineering
segments.summary: The law spurred a 1950s-60s trend of pithy named laws such as the Peter Principle, Boob's law, Franklin's rule, Lincoln's law, and Patton's law. Murphy's Law is also linked to the rise of fail-safe design and redundant systems, and to road-death trends before and after.

segments.title: Fatalism, free will, and the buttered bread
segments.summary: Explores fatalism versus free will as psychological underpinnings of Murphy's Law, using traffic lanes as an example. Kipling's buttered-bread observation is discussed, with the heavier buttered side explaining why bread often lands butter side down.

segments.title: Joel Pell's Murphy's equation
segments.summary: Joel Pell, a biological engineer at the University of British Columbia, devised a 2005 'Murphy's equation' giving the probability that Murphy's Law applies. He tested it on a clutch failure and flashlight scenario, and got a probability of one both times.

segments.title: Personal Murphy's Laws and listener Q&A
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh share personal Murphy's Law examples (house keys, directions, diesel nozzles). They then answer listener questions about Simpsons characters, Hodgman's mustache, and how to find the site and contact info, and sign off.
